summary: San Marino has no airport and no border controls of its own — you enter through Italy, so Schengen rules decide everything: EU/EEA citizens and Schengen visa-waiver nationals walk straight in, while other travelers need an Italian Schengen visa.

fee.notes: Standard Schengen visa fee. San Marino issues no visas of its own. Apply at the Italian embassy or visa center serving your place of residence.

source.name: San Marino Department of Foreign Affairs

passportValidity.text: Schengen rules apply on the way in through Italy: your passport must be valid for at least 3 months beyond your intended departure from the Schengen Area and have been issued within the previous 10 years. EU/EEA citizens can travel on a national ID card.

source.name: San Marino Department of Foreign Affairs

travelInsurance.text: Nothing is checked in San Marino itself. Schengen visa applicants must hold travel medical insurance with at least €30,000 of coverage for the Italian visa; it is recommended for all visitors. Note that San Marino is outside the EU, so check your EHIC arrangements.

source.name: San Marino Department of Foreign Affairs

onwardTicket.text: San Marino performs no entry checks; Italian border rules on onward travel apply when you enter the Schengen Area.

source.name: San Marino Department of Foreign Affairs

proofOfFunds.text: No checks in San Marino itself — Italy's Schengen rules on means of subsistence apply at the external border.

source.name: San Marino Department of Foreign Affairs

currencyLimits.text: The EU rule applies when entering Italy: cash of €10,000 or more must be declared. San Marino applies its own declaration threshold of €10,000 for cash brought into the republic.

source.name: San Marino Department of Foreign Affairs

notes: San Marino sits outside the EU customs union for some goods — duty-free style shopping is popular, and Italian customs can check larger purchases on the way out.

payments.text: Cards and contactless are accepted practically everywhere, as in Italy; a little cash is only useful for the smallest kiosks and parking meters.

safety.text: San Marino is one of Europe's safest destinations — even petty theft is rare, including at the height of the tourist season. Normal precautions are enough.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — San Marino Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: April to June and September to October bring mild weather and thinner crowds on Mount Titano; July and August are hot and busiest, but sunset views over Emilia-Romagna are at their best.

idp.text: San Marino is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

driving.text: San Marino is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for San Marino yet.

tips.text: There are no passport checks between Italy and San Marino. You simply drive or take the bus up from Rimini, and your Schengen entry through Italy covers the visit.
San Marino has no airport or railway — fly to Rimini or Bologna and take the regular Rimini–San Marino bus (about 50 minutes) or drive; parking sits just below the historic center.
Days spent in San Marino count against your 90/180-day Schengen allowance in practice, since entry and exit run through Italy without separate controls.
The tourist office in the old town sells an official souvenir passport stamp for a small fee. It has no legal effect; ask for it on a spare page if you prefer to keep visa pages clean.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for San Marino?
faq.answer: San Marino issues no visas and runs no border controls. Entry is governed by Schengen rules through Italy. If you can enter Italy, whether visa-free or on a Schengen visa, you can visit San Marino.

faq.question: Does visiting San Marino use up a single-entry Schengen visa?
faq.answer: In practice no. There are no controls on the Italy–San Marino border, so you never formally exit the Schengen Area; travelers on single-entry visas visit without any issue.

faq.question: How do I get to San Marino?
faq.answer: There is no airport or train station. Most visitors fly to Rimini or Bologna, then take the direct bus from Rimini (about 50 minutes) or drive. The historic center on Mount Titano is pedestrian — park below and walk or take the funicular.

faq.question: Can I get my passport stamped in San Marino?
faq.answer: Yes — the tourist office by Piazza della Libertà sells a souvenir visa stamp for a few euros. It is purely decorative and causes no problems at other borders, though the cautious ask for it on a spare page.

faq.question: How long can I stay in San Marino?
faq.answer: For visa-waiver and Schengen-visa travelers, your stay is effectively bounded by your Schengen allowance — 90 days in any 180 — since you come and go through Italy. Longer stays require a San Marino residence permit, which is a separate and rarely used process.
